text: White pumps, worn under a burqa, on a young woman who intends to be president of Afghanistan. Nogreh attends a secular girls' school her father knows nothing about, and she questions anyone who might explain how the leaders of other countries actually got elected; she wants the mechanism, not the idea. Her ambition shares a room with her sister-in-law's arithmetic: Leylomah has a baby and no milk, her own hunger having stopped it, and a husband, Akhtar, who has not come back. The Taliban are out of power. The men who were there before them are not. Samira Makhmalbaf, working from Iran in 2003, gives the two women 105 minutes and no hierarchy between them: one problem would take a rebuilt country to answer, the other has to be answered before dark.

In the Poland of 1980, a young man's colleagues are on the take, and vindictive toward anyone who is not. His mother is dying in a hospital where the officials cannot be troubled to attend to her, and between the office and the ward he tries to arrive at a rule for conduct that will hold in both places. The search is quixotic in the exact sense: he is the only person operating under it. Krzysztof Zanussi keeps the question narrow enough to be answerable, not how a person should live but what to do this week, at this job, with this hospital. What wears the young man down is not a conspiracy against him. It is the discovery of how much harm ordinary people are willing to do, and how little it costs them.

The parents are counting the years until they can go home; the daughter is nineteen and already home. They were moved out of Shanghai in the sixties along with other workers' families and resettled in a province, and by the 1980s reform has made return thinkable, provided the household stays portable. Then the daughter attaches herself to a local boy, and the plan acquires a person inside it who does not want it. Wang Xiaoshuai takes 123 minutes over this, time enough for the waiting to stop being a decision anyone made and become the climate the family lives in. Nobody behaves unreasonably. The father wants a city back and believes he is owed it. The girl cannot see why the place she grew up should count as exile, or why her parents' homesickness is her problem.

A man who can no longer want his wife arranges for another man to take an interest in her. The other man is his daughter's lover, so the scheme does not run alongside the family; it runs through it. Kon Ichikawa staged this in 1960 with four people and one house. The premise commits him to bookkeeping rather than passion: who has been told what, whose consent is genuine, which humiliation is expected to produce which effect. The husband who set it going is not the person best placed to keep those accounts, and the daughter is not outside the arrangement either, since it turns on her lover. Everything cold about the film follows from a middle-aged man deciding that his marriage is a problem of engineering, and from the patience with which the household lets him try.

Public speaking was forbidden where he landed, so he set his arguments to music and sang them beside the Salvation Army band. Joe Hill came over from Sweden with his brother early in the last century, lost touch with him within a short time, took the jobs available to a man without a trade, and joined the IWW while the union was banned. Bo Widerberg shot the film in Sweden in 1971 and made it in English, following its subject into the language of the country that took him in. The 118 minutes go on organizing as a form of labour: the jobs, the hours, the songs written because a speech would not have been permitted. His allies accumulate. So, at the same rate, do the people who would prefer he stopped.

The house is large, newly inherited, and its owner fills it with everyone from his office. Rémi is a bachelor and a model employee, the kind of colleague whose life outside the building nobody has had to imagine, and the guest list he draws up includes his superiors. That is the detail that turns a day out into a machine: rank comes along, sits down, and drinks. Claude Goretta plays it as comedy, which is the honest register, since nobody here is undone by an enemy; they are undone by free wine, good company and the sheer length of an afternoon with nothing to do in it. What makes the film uncomfortable is not the behaviour. It is that all of these people have desks, and the desks are still there.

The call-up papers arrive for a young man who had arranged his life in every particular except that one. Benoit had a plan; military service was not in it. He tries what people try in order not to go, and when the evasions are exhausted he goes the other way entirely: nightclubs, drink, drugs, pursued with the diligence he had been saving for the career. Xavier Beauvois shot it in 1995 and let it run 118 minutes, which is the decisive choice. A life spent out every night, filmed at the pace of a life spent out every night, stops reading as appetite well before the man living it stops. Underneath the disorder the planner is still at work. He has only changed the schedule.

He has invited his wife's best friend to dinner while the divorce is being finalized, and he means to tell her everything. Catherine is the wife; Patricia is the friend; Andre is the one talking. What he gives her is his own history in London, from his arrival there as a young man onward: an employer he took up with, a girl set on marriage, a Frenchwoman who was kind to him. René Clément made it in 1954 and built 100 minutes on a narrator with a motive, which alters every woman in the film, since each arrives already shaped by the man describing her, and the listener has heard Catherine's version of the same years. The charm is not faked. That is the difficulty. He is good company across the table, and the evening is an audition.

A photographer whose job is to look is blindfolded, pushed into a car, and driven somewhere he will not be able to name. Patrick Perrault has been covering the war in Beirut in the late 1980s; one afternoon the men with guns come for him. Maroun Bagdadi directed it in 1991, a Belgian production in French, and the premise removes the instrument from the professional: a story about a man who records events, starting at the moment he can record nothing. Most of it has to take place in rooms he is not allowed to see, among people he comes to know by voice. Outside, the city carries on being photographed by others. What he is left holding is his worth to somebody, and worth is not the same thing as protection.

The offence is a manuscript: a law graduate is writing a book, and the government would like him to stop. The government is the Park administration of the mid-1970s, the writer is called Kim, and the subject he will not drop is Jeon Tae-il, a union activist of twenty-two. Park Kwang-su brought it to the screen in 1995 and took the Blue Dragon best film award for it, a domestic verdict on an argument the country had been having with itself. Two periods run at once here: the researcher moving under pursuit, and the young worker whose life he is trying to get onto paper. The second man is available to the first only through documents and other people's memories. That is the ordinary condition of biography, and here it is also the drama.

A hundred and sixty-four minutes, given to a quarrel between the people who own land and the people who work it. Im Kwon-taek made it in 1994 from a story built at river length, and the running time is doing something specific: a grievance handed down from parents to children cannot be staged in ninety minutes without shrinking into an incident. It is filed as a war film as well as a drama, and both labels hold, since the sides had been sorted long before anyone began fighting. The Blue Dragon named it the best film of its year, which is not the ordinary fate of a long rural chronicle. What the scale buys is recurrence: the same argument turning up in a second generation with the terms altered and the positions precisely where they were.

The head falconer demands perfection from everyone within reach and is indifferent to whom his girlfriend spends her nights with. A young man with an interest in ornithology arrives to watch the birds and the men who train them: Hungary, 1970, István Gaál directing. The situation makes the argument without help, a place organized entirely around obedience, run by someone whose work has eaten whatever else he might have had, watched by a visitor with nothing at stake in it. The birds do exactly what is asked of them, and the method that produces that is total. Gaál sets the two facts side by side and declines to reconcile them. Eighty-one minutes, used to keep the visitor exactly where he began: close to the work, and outside it.

The boy who works in the flat sleeps in the kitchen, because that is where the household decided he would sleep. He is not yet a teenager. A cold night, a shut door, carbon monoxide, and from then on the couple who employed him have a police inquiry to fear and neighbours to manage, and the fear arrives well ahead of the grief. Mrinal Sen shot it in Bengali in 1983 and held it to ninety-one minutes, which is exactly long enough for two educated people to talk themselves into being the injured party. Nothing they do is monstrous. It is petty, and it is fluent, and it draws on the same manners that make them agreeable company. The arrangement that put a child in that kitchen had never struck anyone in the house as worth a second thought.

The headmaster needs a name to hand over, and picks a boy who had nothing to do with it. Valerka is expelled, which sounds like the mild end of the punishments available and is not, because the expulsion also settles what will be said about him afterwards. He has been living with his mother, who works as a prostitute; the quarrel that follows sends him out of the house and onto the roads. Vitali Kanevsky filmed this in 1992, the second of three pictures he drew from his own life, and the autobiography shows in what he refuses to treat as exceptional. The bleakness the boy travels through is not a sequence of incidents arranged for him. It is the ordinary condition of the places he passes, one after another, and it does not let up because he is young.
